analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law requiring federal construction contractors to pay locally prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon prevailing wage law was introduced in June 1992, sent to the Senate Labor Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act, on the books since 1931, requires contractors on federally funded construction to pay workers the prevailing local wage for their trade. This bill would wipe that requirement out entirely. Its sponsors argued this would cut federal construction costs, open more contracts to small businesses, and create jobs; critics of such repeals say it would cut the pay of construction workers on federal projects.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had passed, federal construction contractors would have gained the most: they could bid lower by paying less than the local prevailing wage, with the largest advantage going to nonunion firms that already pay below-market wages. Federal taxpayers would have saved some money on construction contracts if contractors passed labor savings through in bids. Building-trade unions and workers who rely on prevailing wage standards would have lost the most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal construction contractors and nonunion bidders

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act outright, ending the requirement that laborers and mechanics on federally financed construction be paid the locally prevailing wage. [S2]
The bill's stated purposes were job opportunities, cost savings on federal construction contracts, more small business participation in federal contracting, and less paperwork for contractors. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federal projects would bear the cost in lower wages, since contractors would no longer be required to pay the prevailing local rate. Union construction trades, which have the most to lose from a wage floor they help sustain, would lose bargaining leverage on federal work.

drawbacks.text: The core effect of repeal would be to remove the only federal guarantee that workers on federal construction jobs earn the local prevailing wage, which would directly reduce pay for those workers. [S2]
Repeal would remove the paperwork and compliance reporting the act imposes on contractors and subcontractors on federal jobs, a real administrative burden the bill's sponsors cited. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings to taxpayers would come directly out of construction workers' pay on federal projects, since the bill's mechanism is letting contractors bid lower by paying less. The benefits to contractors would be immediate and concentrated; the cost would fall on a specific workforce. Anyone weighing this honestly has to ask whether federal construction savings should come from lowering wages rather than from competition among bids that all meet the wage floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 18, 1992, sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, and died there when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote. [S5]

narrative.text: Sen. Larry Craig introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act on June 18, 1992, with Sen. Hank Brown listed as a cosponsor. [S3]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day. [S5]
No further action was taken; the bill never left the committee before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors and opponents of prevailing wage rules got the outcome they wanted without ever having to defend a repeal vote, while the wage floor protecting federal construction workers stayed intact because the bill went nowhere.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal contractors; the wage floor survived

for.name: Sen. Larry E. Craig
for.role: U.S. Senator from Idaho; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act and became its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sen. Hank Brown
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as one of its two cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Edward Kennedy (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action; no markup, hearing, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All three senators associated with the bill were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled Labor Committee that received it never acted on it.

industries.note: Repeal would have let them cut labor costs on federal jobs by paying below the prevailing wage, with the savings coming out of workers' pay. The bill never advanced, so nothing changed.

industries.industry: Building trades unions and their members
industries.note: Davis-Bacon protects the wage floor union contractors bid under; repeal would have undercut union competitiveness on federal work and directly cut pay for covered workers.
